items.stimulus: An archaeologist sketches a broken pottery shard that has three straight edges. She labels its corners $A$, $B$, and $C$ and measures the angles at two of them.
items.stem: In triangle $ABC$, the measure of angle $A$ is $48^\circ$ and the measure of angle $B$ is $67^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $C$?
items.explanation: The angles of a triangle add up to $180^\circ$. The two known angles add up to $48 + 67 = 115$, so angle $C$ is $180 - 115 = 65$ degrees.

A.why: You got the subtraction wrong. $180 - 115$ is $65$, not $55$.

C.why: You subtracted only one of the given angles, $180 - 67 = 113$. You need to subtract both from $180$.

D.why: $115$ is the sum of the two given angles. You stopped before subtracting that sum from $180$.

items.stem: In triangle $PQR$, $PQ = PR$ and the measure of angle $P$ is $40^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $Q$?
items.explanation: Because $PQ = PR$, the angles opposite those sides, $Q$ and $R$, are equal. That gives $40 + 2Q = 180$, so $2Q = 140$ and angle $Q$ is $70$ degrees.

D.why: $140$ is the combined measure of angles $Q$ and $R$. Divide it by $2$ to get each base angle.
